title: Auriga
author: NonAverageJoe2023
selftext:
I’m working on **Auriga**, a voxel rover exploration game about being sent to strange worlds, exploring their environments, drilling for samples, and searching for life.

I’m currently building out the story mode. It begins in 1988, when you’re operating an experimental rover on Mars. Just a few days into the mission, you drill up evidence of ancient life. The project is suddenly shut down and your rover is abandoned.

Hundreds of years later, you wake up.

From there you’ll eventually explore different planets and moons, each with their own environments and hazards. I want the actual science/exploration to be a big part of the game too — sometimes you’ll be following the story, and other times you might drill beneath an ice moon and discover an ecosystem that nobody knew existed.

It’s still early in development and I’m building this as an indie project, but I’m pretty excited about where it’s going.

Would this be something you’d play?

https://nonaveragejoe.itch.io/auriga

comments.author: ActualBrazilian
comments.body: Could have some legal issues with the makers of endless legends maybe? Since the name of their setting is auriga (I'd ask the AI about it before taking my own word)

replies.author: NonAverageJoe2023
replies.body:
It’s actually my first time hearing about it. I searched the name beforehand to make sure there weren’t any other games that had come out using Auriga as their title. (I’ve noticed AI loves to use the same name even among the same developers, or adding things like “-mere” to words and thinking it’s created something unique, Hollowmere, etc.)

I’m definitely no expert on trademark law, but since Auriga is originally the name of a constellation, and in the game you’re referring to it’s apparently the name of the world rather than the actual title of the game, I don’t think it would necessarily be a major issue. Obviously they could still object to it, and trademark law can get complicated, so I wouldn’t pretend to know how that would play out legally.

Either way, if the developers genuinely had a problem with the name of my game, I’d probably just change it rather than create unnecessary hostility over a title.
